en: Milinda-Ṭīkā:
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One,
who incessantly acts for the welfare of the world.
I pay homage to the Hero, the charioteer who tames men, who constantly teaches for the welfare of the world and constantly contemplates for the welfare of the world.
Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, the Lord who knows the fivefold Dhamma,
who reveals the secret Dhamma, and to the Dhamma and the virtues of the virtuous;
and to the Great Elder Nāgasena, who is proficient in the Three Piṭakas;
I shall compose, in brief, this *Milindapañhā-vivaraṇa*,
which elucidates the sweet meaning and clarifies the nature of the questions,
even for that [work] which illuminates the Dhamma through its answers; listen to it with concentrated minds.
1. Likewise, the "Explanation of Miscellaneous Topics" (Pakiṇṇakathāvivaraṇa) and the "Extraction of Jātakas" (Jātakuddharaṇa)—these two are the table of contents.
Furthermore:
The "Connected Text" (Sambandha), the "Words" (Pada), the "Meaning of Words" (Padattha), and the "Word-Analysis" (Padaviggaha).
"The explanation of the meaning is sixfold:
the objection and the resolution"—since this has been stated, the connection should first be understood. And that [connection] is twofold according to the aforementioned "taking up" (*ajjhāhāra*).
This is the exposition of the miscellaneous discussion.

Regarding those [verses]: “That king named Milinda... [etc. ... ‘Sāgara’ here should be understood as connected by ellipsis (*ajjhāhāra*). That King Milinda who was born into the royal family five hundred years after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One—he, the king named Milinda, while exercising sovereignty in the pre-eminent city named Sāgala, approached the Elder Nāgasena.
With what [was he like]? He said: ‘Like the Ganges [approaching] the ocean. Just as the Ganges, or any one of the rivers such as the Yamunā, approaches the ocean...”
"Thus he approached"—this is the meaning. The word *vā* has the sense of inclusion (*veṭha*) and conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Just as one would say "or the Ganges," the vowel *ā* is shortened [to *a*], and thus it is stated as "or indeed the Ganges" (*gaṅgāva*). It is like the word *vā* used in the sense of conjunction in the phrase "like a blue lotus in water.
In the passage "The king, having assailed... [pe] ...in tearing apart," the connection should be understood as being just as previously stated. And that is indeed easy to understand.
Words are fourfold, according to whether they are nouns (*nāma*), prefixes (*upasagga*), particles (*nipāta*), or verbs (*ākhyāta*).

Among these, the noun-word (*nāmapada*) is fourfold, according to whether it is a common noun (*sāmañña-nāma*), a quality noun (*guṇa-nāma*), a conventional noun (*kittima-nāma*), or a derivative noun (*opapātika-nāma*). Likewise, the name "Mahāsammata" (Greatly Elect) is a common noun for a king, because it was established by being elected by the great multitude of people at the beginning of the eon.

One who is a preacher of the Dhamma, one who wears robes made of rags from a dust-heap, one who is a bearer of the Vinaya, one who is versed in the Three Piṭakas, and one who is endowed with faith—[these are examples].
"Faithful" (*pasanno*) is a name derived from a quality; such a name is called a "quality-name" (*guṇanāma*).
Furthermore, on the day a newborn boy’s name is taken, when relatives standing nearby have honored those worthy of offerings, they assign a name, saying, "Let this one be named so-and-so";
this is called a "conventional name" (*kittimanāma*). As for that which was a prior designation, in relation to a subsequent designation...
It falls [into the category of] "conventional expression" (vohāra), where the former conventional expression is subsumed by the latter; that is to say:

just as in the past kappa it was called "moon" and now it is also called "moon," and in the past it was called "sun," "ocean," "earth," and "mountain," and now it is also called "mountain"—this is what is called "spontaneous naming" (opapātika-nāma). This fourfold classification of names is according to the method of the Abhidhamma.
It has been stated. In the *Saddasattha*, however, nouns are said to be fivefold: by way of noun-noun, pronoun, compound noun, derivative noun (*taddhitanāma*), and numeral noun.
All of these should be understood here as appropriate. As for the meaning of the word, "āsajja" means having approached;
"ṭhānāṭhānagate" means having gone to what is possible and what is impossible (i.e., to the grounds and non-grounds).
"Various" (puthu) means of many kinds.

"Arranged in a web of strings" (suttajālasamathita) means arranged and recited by means of the collection of discourses known as the Sutta Piṭaka; or, it refers to those who purify the web of strings by bringing forth the discourses and clarifying the meaning of the strings, and by means of "methods" (nayehi), that is, by the methods of the Abhidhamma, the Vinaya, and so forth, or by logical reasonings (yuttīhi).
"Having resolved" (*paṇidhāya*) means by way of the methods of the Abhidhamma, the Vinaya, and so forth, or by means of logical reasoning (*yutti*).
"Having resolved" means establishing one's own knowledge.
"Having made the mind speak" (*bhāsayitvāna mānasaṃ*) means causing one's own mind to proceed with intensity and repetition, as if it were speaking.

"In the *Kaṅkhāṭhānavidāḷana*": this means in the cause for the splitting apart (*vidāḷana*) of those phenomena such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and other defilements that serve as the basis for doubt (*kaṅkhā*), which is to say, for perplexity (*vicikicchā*). This is the word-meaning (*padattha*).
As for the grammatical analysis (*viggaha*), it should be understood as follows: [it is a compound meaning] "the splitting apart of the grounds of doubt."
"Because he takes away the sinking of people who have fallen into the stream, he is called Miliṇda."
"Sāgaro" means that ocean.
"Abhidhammavinayogāḷhā" means those who have plunged into the Abhidhamma and Vinaya by way of penetrating them.
"Stilled by the web of suttas" means stilled by the web of suttas.
Doubt (*kaṅkhā*) and the grounds for doubt (*kaṅkhāṭhāna*) are "grounds for doubt"; the shattering of these grounds for doubt is "the shattering of the grounds for doubt."

This is the analysis of the title *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* (The Dispeller of Doubts). To the question, "By whom were these five verses composed? the response is: "They were composed by the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa. It is not only these five verses; other preceding and subsequent statements were also uttered by that king of elders.
Among those, regarding the method of connection (*sambandhanaya*):
"A sentence may be a collection of words containing a single verb along with its factors (*kāraka*)," and "For that by which something is connected, even if it stands far away, that [belongs] to it."
Now, therefore, proximity is not the cause for those who are not identical;
"When there is diversity, there is a corresponding diversity of action as is appropriate;
but for that which is covered by a single action, there is never an agency [of individual causes]."
“Sound is the domain of conventional usage; its meaning is manifold from the perspective of ultimate reality;
and its referent is said to be the object of conceptual construction by the intellect.
Having clearly discerned these three characteristics—how the referent and the intrinsic nature are obtained—one should employ words accordingly.

It should be done so. For it is by means of the application of words that the true nature of meanings must be followed, not by means of the true nature of meanings that the application of words is governed;
moreover, teachers residing in various countries explain the meaning of the application of words according to the linguistic usage of their own respective countries.
Here, in our country of Biṅga, the meaning of the application of words is [explained] in accordance with the refined linguistic usage.
It should be spoken. How should it be spoken so that the speech is smooth and enters the hearts of the sons of good family?
If the first [case] is the agent (*kattā*), the second [case] is the object (*kamma*) with its qualification; the verbal form (*kriyāpada*) ending in the first case should be stated.
Or, if the verbal form is stated, the second-case object with its qualification should be stated. If...
A word ending in the nominative case, when accompanied by a qualifier, becomes the object (*kamma*);
its qualifier must be stated with the instrumental case as the agent (*kattā*), and that instrumental expression must be stated as the verb (*kriyāpada*). As for the meaning of the words:
"Signs are to be understood from their own nature, from place and time, and they are analyzed according to words;
it is not by words alone [that they are known]. And:
"But the agent, such as 'self' (sa-āmādi), depends upon the path of other-being (parabhāva)."
"The condition (paccaya) possesses a gender (sadhātu), while the means of accomplishment (sādhana) possesses a meaning (attha);
the word 'gender' (dhātu-sadda) denotes the action (kriyā), while the condition denotes the means of accomplishment.
Its gender-denoting suffixes (liṅga) and case-endings (vibhatti) indicate its meaning."
Having observed these three characteristics, the analysis of the meaning of each word should be stated.
As for the analysis of the words:
"For there may be a cause for running, and there may be a condition for it; there may be a fruit, and there may be a result."
The word *iti* is employed in two senses: for the purpose of indicating "knowing" and as a particle used in every sentence.
Indeed, in every sentence there is both a verb and the word *iti*;
the cause for the arising of the action is illuminated by the word *iti*.
Having first observed these characteristics, one should say:

"This method of the application of words and the application of meanings, which we have explained, is a system of composition that is beneficial in every respect; it should be mastered and observed by sons of noble family.
Hereafter, we shall explain only those points that are not yet clear, both in terms of their meaning and their form.

"Suvibhatta-vīthi-caccara-catukka-siṅghāṭaka" means that which has well-divided streets (*vīthi*), crossroads (*caccara*), junctions (*catukka*), and square intersections (*siṅghāṭaka*). Here, "streets" refers to what is called a *rathikā*;
"crossroads" refers to what is called a *caccara*; "junctions" refers to what is called a meeting point of roads (*maggasandhi*); and "square intersections" refers to what is called a *siṅghāṭaka*.
For this has been stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: [text follows].
“*Racchā*, *visikhā*, *raṭikā*, and *vīthi* are thus described.
A *vyūha* is an unbroken street (*racchā*), while a broken one is a *pathaddhi*.
A *catukka* is a crossroads; it is called a *magga-saṇḍhi* or a *siṅghāṭaka*.”
"Endowed with various kinds of cloth-shops, such as those for Kāsī and Koṭumbara cloths":
herein, "Kāsī cloth" (kāsika) refers to cloth of great value produced in the Kāsī country; "Koṭumbara cloth" (koṭumbara) is cloth born in the region of Koṭumbara. By the word "etc.
(ādi), linen (khoma), cotton (kappāsika), silk (koseyya), wool (kambala), hemp (sāṇa), and jute (bhaṅga) are included. There are also white cloths, which are of a quality corresponding to linen.
Dukūla includes silk, as well as pattunna, paṭṭa, somāra, and Chinese cloth (cīnaja), which are of a similar nature.
For this has been said in the Khuddaka Sikkhāgāthā:
"Dukūla, pattunna, paṭṭa, somāra, cīnaja, that which is produced by supernormal power (iddhija), that given by the gods (devadinna), and whatever else is of a similar nature to these."

And in its commentary it is said: "Because it is made of bark, it is similar to *dukūla*; because it is made of thread produced from fibers of hemp, it is similar to *pattuṇṇa*, *paṭṭa*, *somāra*, and *cīna* cloth;
and because it is made of one or another of those six types of cloth—such as silk-cloth, cloth given by deities through psychic power, or other such cloths—it is similar to them.

Likewise, in the *Milindapañha*, it is stated that there are two kinds of questions: the question on characteristics (*lakkhaṇapañha*) and the question for cutting off doubt (*vimaticchedanapañha*). Herein, of these phenomena...
The inquiry proceeding by way of asking about characteristics is "inquiry into characteristics" (*lakkhaṇapañheyyā*).

It is written in some places as "the inquiry into the characteristics of phenomena" (*dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇapañho*). Regarding the term *ṭhānuppattikapaṭihāno*: at each respective time of investigating profound meaning, there is an arising (*uppatti*) or occurrence (*uppajjana*) in the place (*ṭhāna*) defined as the duty to be performed;
that which has this [arising] is "pertaining to the occasion" (*ṭhānuppattikaṃ*). It "shines forth" (*paṭibhāti*) upon the object.

*Paṭibhānaṃ* means knowledge (*ñāṇaṃ*). One who possesses *paṭibhāna* that arises according to the occasion is called "one whose *paṭibhāna* arises according to the occasion" (*ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhāno*).
Regarding the phrase "capable of [knowing] the past, future, and present," one must supply the words "to know the meanings" (*atthānaṃ jānitum*), or that very reading is intended.
Likewise, in my past existence, I gave gifts, guarded my virtue, developed meditation, and performed what is wholesome.
Now, one who is endowed with knowledge and possesses wealth and fame is capable of knowing the past thus:
"In the future, I must perform meritorious deeds such as giving, so that prosperity may arise; having attained prosperity in existence and being happy, I shall attain final Nibbāna.
In this way, he is said to be capable of knowing the present and the future.

"At the time of performing the activities of the methods for universal application (*samantayogavidhānakiriyā*), the application (*yoga*) should be joined. "Universal" (*samantato*) means from all sides; "everywhere" (*sabbato*) means at all times.
"Application" (*yoga*) is the arranging (*vidhāna*) of all duties to be performed at all times.

"Activity" (*kiriyā*) refers to the arrangement to be performed by means of a method during the preliminary stage, thinking: "I shall do this and that; when this is done, that will come to pass. This [should be applied] precisely at the time of performance.
"It is obtained. The intended meaning is that he was one who acted with circumspection both in the preliminary stage and at the time of performing [the act].
Regarding "seyyathīdaṃ" (that is to say): "I shall analyze those things which were grasped by him as they are," thus it is said;
furthermore, in the *Mahānidāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā*, it is stated in the same way: "seyyathīdaṃ katamāni" (that is to say, which ones?). Some say this.
"What are those five aggregates of clinging? They are as follows: the aggregate of clinging to form," and so on, according to this method.
And among those nineteen synonyms, "Suti" means that by means of it the Dhamma is heard; thus, Suti is the Veda.

"Conventional" (*sammuti*) refers to the literature of words. As for the remaining terms—number and so forth—if they appear in external treatises, they should indeed be easily grasped, since their source is not the [Pali] texts.
"For the purpose of performing the meal-rite" means for the purpose of performing the duties of eating.
"Thus the eye arose all at once" means that, through the power of mindfulness and knowledge resulting from familiarity with the three Vedas in a past birth, it arose all at once.
The eye of knowledge arose for him in such a way that it perceived only a single instance of grasping.
The intention is that the eye of knowledge arose for one who was unable to retain [the teaching] unless it was spoken only once, having been greatly abbreviated.
"Having given the teacher his consent" means: "Teacher, ask me whatever you wish."
"I shall answer it. Tell it to me, for I am unable to explain it myself"—thus he urged his teacher, challenging him to give him the instruction.
For some are able to provide the instruction but not to explain it;
however, the boy Nāgasena was indeed capable of doing both.
"The eye of Dhamma arose" means that the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, having Nibbāna as its object, arose in this manner of arising:
"Whatever kind of conditioned phenomena there may be that have the nature of arising, all those have the nature of cessation.
All that which is a class of conditioned phenomena has the nature of arising; all that has the nature of cessation.
"The thought arose: 'The nature of phenomena is subject to cessation; it is impermanent, having the nature of decay and passing away.
Why did only the knowledge of the Path arise with Nibbāna as its object? Because it arose having shattered the darkness of delusion that conceals it.
[Regarding the word *dosinā*: where "dositā" should have been said, the letter *t* was replaced by *t*, and thus it is written as "dosinā."]
The etymological analysis (*viggaha*) of "chariot" (*ratha*) should be made thus: "It is a chariot because, having mounted it, one goes; it delights the master.
A so-called "royal chariot" is desired as being variegated with all kinds of jewels.

(As for) "cart" (*vayha*): "That by which one carries is a cart. Or, according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It is called a cart (*vayha*) because it covers (*chādeti*)," referring to a vehicle constructed with a roof-covering resembling an upper pavilion, completely draped with garlands and cords.

"Sadāmānikā" refers to a specific type of vehicle constructed according to the method described in the *Aṭṭhakathā*—namely, with rafters made of gold, silver, and other materials on both sides, arranged like the wings of a Garuḍa. Furthermore, the pair consisting of "vayha" and so forth is brought here as a single category.

Regarding the term "Tithakaro": when it is said, "The dwelling in the *titha* is declared to consist of five factors: learning (*uggaha*), hearing (*savaṇa*), questioning (*pucchā*), explaining (*kathana*), and retaining (*dhāraṇa*)," one who, having established himself in such a dwelling in the *titha* and established others therein, becomes a maker of the Dharma-tīrtha by means of making the three Piṭakas proficient in the *titha*.
“Skilled” means one who is capable of understanding the methods for binding and so forth.
“Confident” means one who is free from fear in assemblies.
“Conversant with the conventions” means one who is proficient in the conventions known as local dialects, and who possesses expert knowledge of both one’s own system and other systems.
"Of ready wit" means possessing a ready wit reckoned as excellent speech.

"Wise" means wise by means of the wisdom that is the nourishment of the Dhamma (*dhammoja-paññā*). That which is called the wisdom that is the nourishment of the Dhamma is the wisdom attained through knowledge by which one investigates: "What have I heard? What shall I hear? What is wholesome?
What should I seek? The Venerable Nāgasena also exchanged greetings... [as before] ...and pleased the Elder with those very words of greeting.
The construction is as follows: he won over and gladdened the mind of King Milinda with that very same friendly greeting, and thus exchanged greetings with the king.
“I am known” means that I am recognized and well-known.

Moreover, O Great King, regarding this name "Nāgasena"—the construction is as follows: this name "Nāgasena" is a designation (*saṅkhā*), a conventional term (*samaññā*), a description (*paññatti*), a common usage (*vohāro*), and a mere name (*nāmamattaṃ*).
Here, it is called a "designation" (*saṅkhā*) because it is reckoned (*saṅkhāyati*). It is also called a "discourse" (*saṅkathiyā*);
how is it discoursed upon? For another person, it is reckoned as "self," "being," "person," "individual," "man," "youth," "Tissa," or "Datta," or even as "bed and chair."
"Bedding, a dwelling, a courtyard, a door, or a window"—it is called "designation" (*saṅkhā*) because it is designated in these and many other ways.

It is called "convention" (*samaññā*) because it is rightly known (*sammā ñāyati*). How is it rightly known? As "I," as "mine," and so forth... up to "door" or "window"; it is rightly known thus, hence it is convention.
It is called "description" (*paññatti*) because it is made known (*paññāpīyati*).
(Vohāra): “What is it that is designated? … [as before] … “It is called ‘conventional usage’ (vohāra) because it is used conventionally (voharīyati).
What is it that is used conventionally? ‘I,’ ‘mine,’ … [as before] … or ‘door,’ ‘window’—it is called conventional usage because it is used conventionally.
By these four terms beginning with “designation” (saṅkhā), only the designation of names (nāma-paññatti) is intended, since they are shown to be mere names (nāmamatta).
“If you, O Great King, will converse with me using the discourse of the wise—if you will engage in the dialogue of the wise with me—then both wrapping and unwrapping shall be performed.
Thus, by means of posing questions, wrapping is performed by the wise;
and by means of answering those questions, wrapping is performed by the wise.
"An evasion is also performed;

a refutation is also performed"—thus, by means of this method of refutation, the words for refuting other wise men are performed by other wise men, such as when it is said, "The Elder Nāgasena speaks falsehood," and so forth.
Moreover, every refutation that appears in the *Kathāvatthu* treatise is indeed a refutation.
"Even a withdrawal," O Great King, refers to such a withdrawal as when King Milinda, the preeminent king in Jambudīpa, said: "Why do you speak falsely? and so forth.
"Even a distinction" refers to the distinction known as the praise of virtues, such as: "The mind of the Sage is endowed with samādhi;
through his action and proficiency, he praises those who have attained the Dhamma and are perfected in knowledge and conduct. But here, [the phrase] means "you are fit."

"Bhante," and so forth, refers to the excellence of acceptance; that is, the excellence of acceptance consisting in the praise of virtues, as expressed in such passages as, "The mind of the Sage is perfected... you rejoice in those who have turned toward the Dhamma.
Here, however, it is the phrase beginning with, "It is well, Great King, that you know the chariot.
"Claiming one thing" means claiming some single excellent object, such as a precious gem and the like, as being auspicious.
Whether it exists or does not exist, they profess [this]. On the first day, three questions were asked by the King:
the question on names and designations, the question on the seven-year-old, and the question of examination.
"Venerable Nāgasena, I shall ask you... ... "But what, Great King, was asked by you?"—this is the third, the question of examination.
It is called a "question of investigation" because it was asked by way of inquiry for the purpose of knowing the *ṭhānuppattika-paṭihāna* (the miracle of appearing at the right place).
When [the Elder] said, "Thus have I been questioned, venerable sir," this was said by the King with reference to the two questions he himself had previously asked.
When [the Elder] said, "It has been answered by me," this too was said by the Elder with reference to the two questions he himself had previously answered.
"‘Nāgasena, Nāgasena,’ he departed while reciting [this name]," says this to show that King Milinda had great esteem and reverence for the Elder Nāgasena.

For the Master Buddhaghosa has stated: "A person lacking respect, even upon seeing, hearing, or knowing a person worthy of honor, becomes as if not seeing, not hearing, and not knowing them. Herein, this is the meaning of the words: [he departed] while reciting [the name].
He is called a *nāga* because he does not come (*āguṃ*) to commit evil. He is called a *sena* because by means of it, those who oppose his speech lie down and sleep;
thus, one who is both a *nāga* and a *sena* is *Nāgasena*. Among the four types of names—such as the name based on commonality (*sāmañña-nāma*)—this is a name based on renown (*kittināma*).
"The Elder thoroughly rejoiced" means with the words "Excellent! Very well! The question asked while on the road is the "question at the opportune time."
"What is this 'Nāgasena'? he asked. "Which phenomenon (dhamma) in this statement is called Nāgasena? [The Elder replied: "The life-principle (jīva);
it is the wind that has become the life-principle.
"In-breathing and out-breathing—these are the bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra). By means of this Abhidhamma discourse, [the Elder] [referred to] the infinite body.
"These winds that enter within and exit without, called inhalation and exhalation, are conditioned by the body made of kamma;
therefore they are bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra). For this very reason, when one says 'Nāgasena, Nāgasena,' one seizes a mere name;
a person or a soul is not to be apprehended. Thus the Elder delivered a discourse on the Abhidhamma.
‘He declared his status as a lay follower’—by means of the four ways of going for refuge, namely: by surrendering oneself, by entering into discipleship, by prostration, and by formal undertaking;
specifically, by the undertaking [of the precepts], he established his status as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) toward the Triple Gem and the Elder, saying:
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha,” and that...
"I go for refuge; please accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.
This is the fourth question concerning the infinite body (*anantakāya*).
Regarding the phrase "In what does conversation arise?": in what cause or condition acting as a sign does conversation arise? What is its purpose?

The intention of the phrase “kathāsallāpo” (discourse and conversation) is as follows: it should be understood that this was said by the King for the purpose of granting a formal inquiry (*anuyoga*) and for the purpose of providing an opportunity for questioning.

Therefore, with the words, “If you have a need, O Great King, let there be a discourse and conversation,” the Elder grants both the inquiry and the opportunity to the King; thus [it is said], “if you have a need.”
"Furthermore, *payojana* [is used] in the sense of sound, denotation, increase, wealth, wind, cause, destruction, benefit, and the western mountain.
Among these meanings thus stated, both "purpose" (*payojana*) and "benefit" (*hita*) are applicable here. Of these, the fruit is both mundane and supramundane.
The purpose (*payojana*) is indeed the growth of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). It is called "beneficial" (*hita*) because it promotes (*hinoti*) and brings about the attainment of desired fruits.
It refers to the mundane and supramundane causes such as generosity, virtue, and so forth.
As for the question "In what?": in what—namely, in Nibbāna, which is designated as the unconditioned element and as the fruit—would this present suffering cease?
"Parinibbāna through non-clinging" refers to the parinibbāna characterized by the fruit of arahantship. For nibbāna is twofold: unconditioned parinibbāna and parinibbāna through non-clinging.
Among these, the unconditioned element is called "unconditioned parinibbāna" because it is devoid of conditions such as ignorance.
[The other] is called "parinibbāna through non-clinging" because it is devoid of clinging, which is comprised of the defilements.
The fruit of arhatship is called parinirvāṇa through non-clinging.
"Led away by kings" means oppressed by kings or afraid of kings.
"Distressed by debt" means oppressed by debt.
"By the knowledge of exposition (*byākaraṇa-ñāṇa*), you are skilled; in the *Aṅguttaraṭīkā*, [it says] 'proficiency in exposition' (*samatho*). It is indeed appropriate to say 'capable' as well.
This is the fifth question on going forth (*pabbajjā-pañha*).
"With clinging" (*sopādāno*) means "with defilements" (*sakileso*).
The sixth question: On Burning Away.

"By means of wise attention" (*yoniso manasikārena*) means by way of the method and path characterized by recollection that [perceives] "it is impermanent, it is suffering," which is the attention that establishes the object.
The seventh question: On Attention.

"Having the characteristic of exertion" means having the characteristic of exerting itself toward the object by way of joining with the associated mental states, or having the characteristic of grasping.
This is the eighth question on the characteristic of attention.

"That which is the pillar of virtue, possessing the excellent Pātimokkha" refers to that which is designated as the restraint of virtue through the Pātimokkha, occurring only upon the arising of a Buddha.
The virtue of morality that has arisen establishes itself by way of being a support for the eleven wholesome states beginning with faith;
thus, it is both a *nissaya-paccaya* (support-condition) and, in the sense of being a powerful cause, an *upanissaya* (decisive-support). It is like the earth, which is the foundation for all beings.
This is the ninth question: the characteristic of the establishment of morality.

"Having seen with the eye of knowledge that the minds of others are liberated" means: having seen with the eye of knowledge that the minds of other noble ones (ariya) are specifically intent upon and inclined toward the fruits, such as the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).
This is the tenth question concerning the characteristic of faith.
"All wholesome states" (sabbe kusalā dhammā) means: all mundane wholesome states that have arisen do not decline.
The eleventh question, on the characteristic of energy (*vīriya*).

"Having the characteristic of not floating" means having the characteristic of plunging in the sense of entering into the object. "A phenomenon with a counterpart" (*sappaṭibhāga*) means those that proceed together with a counterpart—that is, an adversary. The bright (*sukka*) has the dark (*kaṇha*) as its counterpart; thus it is "with a counterpart.
If there is a reading such as "dark and bright with counterparts," it is indeed very good.
"Apilāpeti" means it penetrates in the sense of entering into.
"The courses of beneficial and harmful phenomena" refers to the accomplishment—defined as the state of yielding desirable or undesirable results—of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
"Sabbathaka" means that which is appointed to all duties, or that which is required in all instances of skillful action.
The twelfth question: on the characteristics of truth.
"Tappamukhāvā" means as if headed by the king.
The thirteenth question: on concentration.
"That which arises is itself that": whatever ultimate phenomenon (paramatthadhamma) such as earth-contact and so forth arises, it is precisely a phenomenon that has arisen before.
The fourteenth question: On the Characteristic of Wisdom.
The fifteenth question: On Performing Various and Single Functions.
The first chapter, consisting of fifteen questions, is completed.

[When you said,] "But what, venerable sir, would you say when this was spoken?"—referring to that time when you were young, tender, intoxicated, and lying on your back, and now you are that same person grown to adulthood—in this statement, by way of my questioning, [I asked:
"What would you say?"... [the rest of the sentence continues].
The construction is: "When this has been said, what would you say?

In the second chapter, however, the first is the question on the continuity of phenomena (*dhammasantati*), and the second is the question on knowing without a reflected image (*na paṭisadahanajānana*).
"Sakiccaya" means the function of illuminating its own object.
"Ālimpanaṃ vijjhāpetuṃ" means to extinguish the fire.
This is the third question concerning the cessation of wisdom.

"Just as a hired laborer," means: just as a hired laborer, while performing his work for hire, receives his wages little by little (*nibbisam*) and finds no joy in living, nor does he find joy in death, but simply awaits the time of death;
even so, I await and look forward to the time of death—this is the intended meaning.
The Fourth Question on Final Nibbāna.
If wholesome [states] are not suffering: if a pleasant feeling were wholesome, that wholesome feeling would not be of the nature of suffering.
If it were so, it would not be wholesome. It is not tenable that "the wholesome is suffering," meaning that the wholesome is of the nature of suffering.
"It is not logical to say that such a statement is untenable.
'Wholesome [states] are not suffering, because they are mutual opposites'—this is the King's intention. However, their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is not thus.

For wholesome pleasant feeling is suffering by way of the suffering inherent in formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha) and also by way of the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). It is also suffering in the sense of the mental distress (domanassa) associated with renunciation, yet it is wholesome in the sense of being blameless (anavajja)."
The Elder thought, "If I say 'it may be wholesome,' when the king asks me the question regarding the iron ball and the lump of snow, the king will answer incorrectly.
I shall then attribute fault to him. The king will answer that incorrectly; I shall then attribute fault to him.
Unable to resolve it, the king will entreat me to speak the truth. Then the king [will realize] that truth."
Thinking, "I shall convince him," he said, "What do you think, Great King? and so forth.

When the Elder had uttered this interrogative statement, "Great King, would both of them burn it?", the King—having heard that there is a fire-element known as cold and heat, and bearing in mind the state of hard chewing even for a cold lump of snow—[responded] from his knowledge of discerning the predominance of the elements (*dhātu-ussada*).
"Having contradicted [my statement], Venerable Sir, would you burn both of us?"—this was the contradictory reply.
"No, Venerable Sir"—this was the King’s rejection through denial.
"Understand the refutation"—this was the Elder’s statement. Because of your subsequent "No," which contradicts your prior admission of "Yes."
"Venerable sir," he replied; yet his later admission did not accord with his former one. Therefore, he fell into that refutation.
"Accept this refutation, this fault, this transgression!"—thus [he spoke].
Now, making that refutation manifest by way of showing the state of heat in both and by way of showing the state of coldness in both, he said: "If it is hot, it burns," and so forth.
Likewise: “If it is the heat that burns”—if both [the iron and the heat] possess the nature of heat, then they burn.
“If it is the heat that burns” is a statement setting aside [the opponent's position].

“And not those two” is a statement attributing a fault [to their position]. Therefore, the statement “because of the hot nature of both, both of these burn” does not arise—that is, it is not applicable or consistent—with the burning of the nature of heat itself.
If it is argued that "if the cold burns," meaning that the coldness of both [fire and water] burns, then it does not follow;
for that reason, because of the coldness of both, the statement that "both of them burn" cannot be maintained as it is illogical for coldness to burn.
Furthermore, making this fault more evident, the Elder asks: "For what reason..."
But he said, "Both of them burn, O Great King," and so forth.
"Why? For what reason? means: for what cause do both of them burn?
"Therefore it is not tenable" means: for that reason, because of the state of one being hot and the other being cold.
The statement made by you, "both of them burn," is neither logical nor tenable. You have stated, "both of them burn," yet what you have said is inconsistent.
You have indeed stated that "the wholesome is suffering," yet you say that it is not tenable to state "the wholesome is suffering.
Why do you say this? You say that a statement which is fit to be made is not tenable. To speak...
Seeing the flaw in his own position through the Elder’s words, “You say that an improper statement is appropriate,” and being unable to avoid it,
the opponent, feeling dejected, requested the Elder to speak further on the matter, saying, “I am not capable,” and so forth. “By you,
the speaker” means by one who speaks with logical, profound, and diverse eloquence.

"Speak the meaning well; I entreat you, speak it well. "Whether pleasant feelings are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—speak the meaning of this question I have asked, teach it. I am in need of the meaning; what is the use of dispute? This is the intended sense.

"Dependent on the household" means dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure which are like a house, occurring with reference to them. "'Dependent on renunciation' [means... [The remainder of the passage follows].
"Come!
Going forth is the first treasure, Nibbāna and insight;
all wholesome states are called 'renunciation.'"
In the renunciations described— namely, those consisting of the wholesome states of insight into Nibbāna—
they are dependent upon renunciation.
This is the fifth question on pleasant feeling.
And this [work] is even more profound than other questions; therefore, noble sons, rather than being satisfied with the mere extent of what has been stated by me,

you should reflect upon it again and again by the power of your own wisdom, examine the preceding and following parts, and grasp only that meaning which is more logical than the meaning I have expressed.

"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): in the sense of bending (*namana*) and in the sense of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*) are "name. Here, "name" refers specifically to resultant name.

"Form" (*rūpa*) is so called in the sense of being affected by cold and so forth. In the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*), form consists of the ninety-six categories of produced form (*nipphanna-rūpa*);
in the secondary sense (*pariyāyato*), it also includes the ten kinds of unproduced form (*anipphanna-rūpa*), namely the decads of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and sex.

There are seven sets of eight, three sets of eight produced by mind, temperature, and nutriment, and two kinds of sound—namely, that produced by mind and that produced by temperature—making ninety-six categories of material phenomena (*rūpa*).
However, here it is *kamma*-born materiality that is intended.
By means of that *kamma*, another name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is produced; thus, by that wholesome or unwholesome *kamma*, another name-and-form [arises].
One correlates another future name-and-form, included within the realms of happy or miserable destinies, with this present name-and-form. The construction is as follows:

"Venerable sir, would a person, without abandoning or relinquishing the previous mango seed—which has become the fundamental cause—be able to obtain a fruit from the later mango that has been produced?
This is the sixth inquiry concerning the correlation of name-and-form.
"Adorned with a simile as its ornament":
"Adhikāraṃ" means a great honor or service. It should be understood that this seventh question is asked again because of a desire to hear the simile; it was asked once more.
This is the seventh question concerning a further response.
The eighth question is on name-and-form.
The ninth question is on the periods.
This is the second chapter containing nine questions.
The first question in the third section, concerning the inquiry about the root of the world.
"Having drawn a wheel upon the earth" means having drawn it thoroughly by way of repeated revolutions of the revolving wheel.
The second question, concerning the non-apprehension of a prior limit.

The aggregates (*khandhā*) are the seeds of suffering; that is to say, as the basis for reconnection (*paṭisandhi*), the aggregates act as the very seeds by way of being the root cause for the entire mass of the suffering of the process-of-becoming (*pavatti*).
Thus, the intention is that it is possible to increase the suffering of the process-of-becoming through this reconnection-bond known as the limit of moments (*khaṇakoṭi*).
The third question, on the increase of the koṭis.
"When, Great King, there is the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises"— here, according to the method in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*,
among the many eye-sensitivities that are co-nascent, it is that eye which is clear and lucid that [serves as the basis] for visual consciousness.

The condition of dependence (*nissayapaccaya*). Because of the use of the singular number in the phrase "in the eye" (*cakkhusmiñca*), and because of the use of the plural number in the phrase "and in visible forms" (*rūpesu ca*), it should be understood that even many visible forms serve as the pre-arising condition (*purejātapaccaya*) for eye-consciousness by virtue of their specific individual nature.
This concludes the fourth question regarding the perception of "there is something."

"O Great King, it is indeed formations themselves that are born; thus, here the proximate condition exists in the past. 'They have arisen in the past'—this is the meaning. And this verse is a parallel verse.
The verse beginning with ‘ahuvā sambhoti’ should be understood as a momentary verse. For in this way, the preceding and following [texts] are consistent. (The upper fire-stick):
The stick that performs the function of rubbing together with the lower fire-stick is called the *uttarāraṇi*."
The fifth is the Question of Bhavantaja, together with the Simile of the Child.
The sixth is the Question of Vedagu.
The seventh is the Question of Eye-consciousness and so forth.

"Characterized by contact" means characterized by contact with the mental object. Regarding the phrase "just as the eye": here, both the sensitivity of the eye (*cakkhuppasāda*) and eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) are included.
"Having the function of impingement": when these objects and faculties impinge, this [consciousness] possesses that function;
and when eye-consciousness is also present, its function is the impingement upon the mental object.

The phrase "of this" (*etassa*) is thus obtained. Furthermore, the expression "the essence of collision" (*saṅghaṭṭanarasa*) is found in the case of contact belonging to the five doors, but not in the case of contact belonging to the mind door;
such is the meaning stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*. This concludes the eighth question on the characteristic of touching (*phusanalakkhaṇa*).
The ninth question: on the characteristic of feeling.
The tenth question: on the characteristic of perception.
The eleventh question: on the characteristic of volition.
The twelfth question: on the characteristic of consciousness.
A carpenter applies well-prepared timber to the frame; that is, people apply, cause to reach, and insert well-prepared timber into a frame.
The thirteenth question: on the characteristic of applied thought (*vitakka*).
The fourteenth question: On the characteristic of investigation (*vicāra*).

The third chapter, containing fourteen questions, is completed. "Having analyzed" (*vinibbhujitvā*) means having separated them one by one from each other; "having dissected" (*vinibbhajitvā*) means having divided them individually.
Among the chapters, the first question, which exceeds [the others], is the first analytical question (*vibhajja-pañha*).
"Is it not the case that only salt should be brought? [The Elder replied: "Only pure salt should be brought by means of carts and oxen.
"It is not possible, O Great King, to bring salt alone"—by this reading it should be understood; however, the negative particle (*na*) appears in the manuscript.
This is the second question on salt, spoken first by the Elder for the purpose of firmly establishing the King in the characteristics of the Dhamma.
Thus far, forty-three questions have been completed.
In the fourth section, O Great King, it was stated: "The five sense-bases of beings destined for the states of deprivation are produced by various karmas, not by a single karma.
The five sense-bases of beings included within the happy destinies [are likewise produced by various karmas].
These [material phenomena] are produced by various wholesome kamma, specifically by that single kamma which generates a rebirth-linking. In the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā*,

by the statement, “At the moment of rebirth-linking, sublime volition is a condition for the material phenomena of past deeds (*kaṭattārūpa*) by way of kamma-condition,” it is understood that all material phenomena of past deeds existing at the moment of rebirth-linking have kamma as their condition.
"If there were the arising of faculties through various volitions at that time, then the *kaṭattārūpa* (kamma-born matter) produced by both very limited and sublime kamma would result;
yet a single rebirth-linking does not arise from multiple kamma-formations.
Thus it is said: "The arising of multiple faculties occurs together with a single kamma. Having investigated this, one should accept whatever is most logical.
In this regard, what is the manner of investigation?
The faculties of sublime beings are produced by a single kamma capable of generating rebirth-linking.

However, the Elder Nāgasena was an Arahant, one whose taints were exhausted and who knew the Buddha’s thought; thus, in accordance with the Buddha’s intention, he [described] the faculties of sense-sphere beings as being produced by various kammas.
It should be understood as "arising.
This is the first question on the sense bases arising from various karmas.
"Noble birth" (mahākulīnatā) means high birth; or that very reading [is correct]. [The qualities of] health, complexion, happiness, wealth, noble birth, and wisdom—these five...
"These fourteen questions were also elucidated in the Subha Sutta"—this verse was spoken by the ancients for the purpose of making it easy to recite and master.
This was the second question concerning the diversity among human beings.
"What is the use of striving beforehand?"—is there any purpose in exertion, that is, in performing an action accompanied by prior effort?

"An 'one who does what should not be done' (akiccakaro)" means here that he does not perform the task (kicca) consisting of the desired fruit; thus he is an "akiccakaro. This is an irregular compound (ayuttasamāsa), similar to such expressions as "one who does not eat the food of the dead" (asaddhabhoji).
"Hungry" (bubhukkhito) means overcome by hunger.
This is the third question concerning the performance of duties at the proper time.
"Being cooked" means being burned by the fires of hell.

"He does not die for the time being" means that for that long, that being in hell does not undergo death. "By the weight of karma" means by the previously accumulated karma which serves as the primary cause.
This is the fourth question, concerning the lack of sinking [into the fire].
The fifth question: On the Support of the Path of Space and Water.
"Clinging" (*ajjhosāya*) means having swallowed with craving and having brought it to completion.
The sixth question: On Cessation and Nibbāna.
‘Dhammas to be directly known’ means those dhammas to be known by means of the distinguished knowledge of the Four Truths; that is, the dhammas of the Four Truths.
The seventh question is on the attainment of Nibbāna.
The eighth question is on the knowledge of Nibbāna.
The Fourth Chapter: On Eight Questions. In the Fifth Chapter:
The First Question on the Existence of a Buddha;
the Second Question on the Supremacy of the Buddha.
"Is it possible to know that the Buddha is unsurpassed?"—this was what the King had previously asked the Elder, "Is the Blessed One the unsurpassed Buddha?
Why was it stated again? The previous question was asked with the Elder’s own knowledge in mind;
the subsequent question was asked with the knowledge of all the wise in mind. The latter question was asked so that all the most learned might understand.
It should be understood that [the question] was asked after having made an agreement.
The third "Unsurpassed Question of the Buddhas" is concluded.

Regarding the phrase "The Guide of the Buddhas": it is called *netti* because by means of it one is led (*neti*) to Nibbāna in the world including the devas; thus, it refers to the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas.

“*Paññatti* means that by this [means] the instruction of the Blessed One is made known; it is a designation (*paññatti*). ‘The Buddha’s *paññatti*’ is *buddha-paññatti*, referring to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
Why did the Elder say, ‘O Great King, this Dhamma has been seen by me,’ without first stating, ‘As long as life lasts, the disciples must conduct themselves [accordingly]’?
Because the King had personally realized the Elder’s state of vision regarding the Dhamma, he [the Elder] spoke with such diverse eloquence.”
He asked because he desired to hear, not out of a wish to display his own knowledge; the Elder, knowing his underlying intention, spoke thus.
For one who has not yet seen the Dhamma is able to conduct himself according to the Buddha’s guidance and the Buddha’s dispensation for as long as life lasts.
This is the fourth question: "The Question on Seeing the Dhamma."
The fifth question: On Entering the New.

"Is one who has mastered the Vedas (vedagu) found?"—this question was also asked previously. Why was it asked again? The previous question was asked with reference to the "living being who has mastered the Vedas" (jīvavedagu).
This [present question], however, refers to the "person who has mastered the Vedas" (puggalavedagu), as stated in the passage beginning, "Those brahmins who have mastered the Vedas... and so forth.

Having accepted [the conventional designation], he was questioned. He asked with the intention of attributing a fault to the Elder’s position should he reply, "In all cases, the Veda-knowing one is not found.

But the Elder, having accepted the designation of the non-existent based on the existent, said: "In the ultimate sense, O Great King, the Veda-knowing one is not found. The Elder’s intention was: "He is not found in the ultimate sense, but he is found from the standpoint of conventional usage (vohāra)."
The sixth question: On the person who knows through experience.

"Not by him planted... means those mangoes were taken away; those mangoes were taken away by a man, yet they were not planted by that man who was their owner, nor did they become mango trees planted by him.
This is the seventh question: concerning this body.
The eighth question is on "wherever.
The ninth question is on "reborn" and "knows.
The tenth question is on "the Buddha exists."
The fifth chapter, consisting of ten questions.
"It trickles out from all sides" means that it causes impurities such as feces and urine to flow out from every direction.
In the sixth chapter, the first question concerns the body being unlovely.
The second question: On the Appropriate Time.
Regarding the phrase "adorned with the thirty-two [marks]," the specific nature of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man has appeared in many suttas and is thus well-known;
however, his beautiful form endowed with the eighty minor characteristics is not well-known, appearing only in the *Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*.
Therefore, we shall demonstrate them. What are the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*)?

They are: well-rounded fingers, tapering fingers, rounded fingers, copper-colored nails, elevated nails, glossy nails, concealed ankles, level feet, a gait like that of an elephant, a gait like that of a lion, a gait like that of a swan, and a gait like that of a bull.

The quality of having limbs that curl to the right; the quality of having beautiful, rounded knee-caps all around; the quality of having fully developed male characteristics; the quality of having an unblemished navel; the quality of having a deep navel;
the quality of having a navel that curls to the right; the quality of having thighs like the trunk of a golden plantain tree;

the quality of having arms like those of the elephant Erāvaṇa; the quality of having well-proportioned limbs; the quality of having smooth limbs; the quality of having clean limbs; the quality of having well-defined limbs; and the quality of having all limbs that are neither too fleshy nor too emaciated.

The state of having limbs free from depression; the state of having limbs devoid of moles and the like; the state of having limbs that are gradually tapering and beautiful; the state of having pure limbs;

the state of having limbs possessing the strength of a thousand million elephants; the state of having a prominent nose; the state of having a well-proportioned nose; the state of having lips with red teeth visible; the state of having very white teeth;

the state of having perfectly pure sense faculties; the state of having rounded canine teeth; the state of having red lips with symmetrical reflection; the state of having a long face; the state of having deep lines on the palms; and the state of having long lines.

The quality of having prominent eyebrows; the quality of having well-formed, beautiful arches to the eyebrows; the quality of having a perfectly rounded body; the quality of having full cheeks; the quality of having long and wide eyes;

the quality of having eyes possessing the fivefold clarity; the quality of having eyelashes that curve upward at the tips; the quality of having a tongue that is soft, thin, and red; the quality of having a long tongue; the quality of having long and beautiful ears;

the quality of having no visible veins on the neck; the quality of having no visible sinews; the quality of having a head as beautiful as a parasol and peaceful; and the quality of having a forehead that is long, broad, and radiant.
Well-shaped eyebrows; dark eyebrows; delicate limbs; exceedingly radiant limbs; exceedingly gentle limbs; exceedingly pure limbs;
soft limbs; smooth limbs; fragrant and slender [limbs]; even body hair; the ability to maintain extremely subtle inhalation and exhalation;
a well-proportioned face; a fragrant mouth; a fragrant forehead; deep blue hair; and hair curling to the right.
The hair of his head is well-shaped; his hair is glossy; his hair is soft; his hair is untangled; it is adorned with the jewel of a crest-ornament.
This is the third question on the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The fifth question is on the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
The sixth is the question on seeking tears.
The eighth is the question on experiencing flavors.
The eighth is the question on wisdom.
The ninth question is on saṃsāra.
The tenth question is on mindfulness (sati).
Thus, venerable Nāgasena, all mindfulness arises knowing its object; there is no such thing as "raw" or unrefined mindfulness. Thus [it is].
In the mode of reflection, all mindfulness arises clearly manifest by itself, without depending on instruction from another, as one who fully understands.
There is no such thing as "mindfulness" that is accompanied by effort—meaning, that which is characterized by striving and instruction from another.
This concludes the eleventh inquiry: the Question on Mindfulness as Full Understanding.
The sixth chapter, together with eleven questions.

"Abhijānato" means from one who knows the specific distinction accompanied by mindfulness (*sati*). "Kaṭumikāya" means from the state of toil (*kaṭumikā*), which is defined as oppression and harsh instruction.
"Olārikaviññāṇato" means from consciousness occurring in relation to a gross object. "Ahitaviññāṇato" means from consciousness characterized by harm, that is, suffering (*dukkha*).
"From the consciousness that has arisen" means from the consciousness that has already occurred. "From a similar sign" means from a similar object.
"From a dissimilar sign" means from objects such as names, colors, and so forth, which are mutually distinct. "From the recognition of speech" means from the recognition known as another's discourse.
"From a characteristic mark" means from marks such as a bull, a cart, teeth, or pimples. "From a reminder" means by being reminded by others. "From calculation" means from the learning of letters.
"From cultivation" means from the cultivation known as direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). "From being bound in a book" means from the retention of the words of instruction written in a book.
"From what has been experienced" means from having previously experienced the six objects. "They bind" means they press down.
"Because of training in writing" means because of training in the script.
In the seventh chapter: the first is the Question on the Modes of Mindfulness;
the second is the Question on the Hundred Years;
the third is the Question on the Future.
The fourth is the Question on the Distant Brahma-world.
The fifth is the Question on the Brahma-world and Kashmir.
The sixth is the Question on the Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
The seventh question is on greater merit.
The eighth question is on knowing and not knowing.
The ninth question is on Uttarakuru.
The tenth is the Question on Long Bones.
The eleventh is the Question on Inhalation and Exhalation.
The twelfth is the Question on the Ocean.
The Thirteenth Question: On Single Flavor.
Regarding the statement "There is no second cutting by means of wisdom," that which is a cutting together with wisdom—those two are not a cutting;
thus it is said. The Fourteenth Question: On Cutting. The Fifteenth Question: On the Living Being. The Sixteenth Question: On What is Difficult to Do.
This was spoken first by the Elder. This is the seventh chapter, containing sixteen questions.

Regarding the phrase "sampati kā velā," the construction is: "What time has now arrived? "Gamissantī" means "they will go with you. "Bhaṇḍato" means from the storehouse. "Rājadeyyāni" means things belonging to the king.
"The king [was] pleased by his exposition of the questions" refers to the exposition of the eighty questions given by that Elder Nāgasena.
The king was pleased. Regarding the statement "he remained during the internal discourse," the questions were answered on the first day.
From the time of the meal in the palace until the end of the first watch of the night, three days passed while the questions on the internal discourse were being answered.
There were three questions on the external discourse. Together with those, there were ninety-one questions in total.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Milindapañha*, adorned with eighty-nine questions.

However, in the *Meṇḍakapañha*, the term *bhassappavādī* refers to one whose habit is to speak speech characterized by appropriate discourse due to skill in conventional expression (*vohārakusalatā*). The term *vetanaḍī* refers to one whose habit is to speak words that contradict the doctrine of the Elders (*theravāda*).

"Dwelling in his shadow" means: he dwells in the "shadow" consisting of the teacher's words of instruction—characterized by compassion and wisdom—which are reckoned as beneficial, appropriate, and based on similes concerning what should and should not be done;
[the disciple] being endowed with the qualities of good fortune such as those described in the verse:
"Though lacking faith, that wise man, adorned with the jewels of virtues such as practice of the Dhamma, reverence, and wisdom, is one who faces the Deathless."
For those [questions] proceed from the Elder’s knowledge of compassion (*karuṇā-ñāṇa*) as if from his mental body (*nāmakāya*), like a shadow proceeding from his physical body.
He "saw the profound questions of Meṇḍaka" means that he saw them with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*).

Alternatively, because they were spoken by Senaka and others in many ways and were of a marvelous nature, they are similar to the questions of Meṇḍaka. Alternatively, because they possess dual forms...
It is also appropriate to say that this question is like the fight between the two bulls.
There is a statement made by way of a method (*pariyāya*); for instance, Ānanda, there is the methodical statement beginning with, "Two kinds of feeling have been taught by me by way of a method.
How is it to be known that this teaching possesses both the methodical and the non-methodical aspects? For equanimous feeling (*upekkhā-vedanā*) is peaceful...
"‘The Blessed One has spoken of sublime happiness’—this is the figurative method (pariyāya).
There is also the literal expression (nippariyāya), such as: ‘Bhikkhus, there are here three feelings: pleasant, painful, and neutral feeling.
How is the literal nature to be known? For the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of feeling is threefold."
This is indeed the non-figurative sense.
"It was spoken with a foundation," monks; by these three points the people of Jambudīpa surpass the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and the humans of Uttarakuru.
By which three? [They are: "They are brave, they possess mindfulness, and here is the dwelling in the holy life," and so forth.
"Having established [the teaching], it was said: 'Herein lies the dwelling in the holy life (brahmacariyavāsa).
This refers to the dwelling in the holy life of renunciation (pabbajjā-brahmacariyavāsa), not the dwelling in the holy life of the Path (magga-brahmacariyavāsa).

Here, the interpretable meaning (neyyattha) has not been included; that too should be brought forward and shown. Such as the interpretable statement: 'Whatever is felt, all that is suffering,' and so forth. Also, 'Even pleasure...'"
"Feeling is impermanent, conditioned," and so forth— this should be understood according to the literal sense as "definitive speech" (nītārtha).
"That which is both of interpretable meaning and spoken with a purpose,
and that which is both spoken by way of a method and spoken according to its own nature."
"Thus, having clearly discerned all that which is spoken by the Victor in the Dispensation according to its fivefold classification,
the wise one should explain its meaning"— by this it is meant that one should not act in secrecy;
that is, one should not utter words that conceal the true meaning.
"It ripens as heavy" means it undergoes maturation through its heaviness; the intention is that it becomes manifest through its state of solidity (*dadha*).
"By way of brevity" means by way of having little elaboration (*appaññatā*).
"By way of duration" means...
"‘Grasping, hearing, questioning, explaining, and retaining—
by means of these five factors alone, dwelling for three years is proclaimed. Thus it is by way of such a three-year residence as has been described.

"Attendance upon the affectionate" means by way of associating with a beloved person. "Having a wise companion" means one whose companion is wise—that is, one whose companion possesses discerning wisdom.
"Do not fear, but rather advance": when fear arises from self-reproach and so forth, do not be afraid for this reason.
Having performed merit, having created a refuge from fear, endowed with knowledge, and established in right application, before long one will [attain] the mundane and supramundane chariot.
"He approaches" means he will approach or proceed.
"Addressing" (*ālāpa*), some say, refers to the first form of greeting (*āmantanā*). "The word 'Raṭṭhaka'" is an instance of such addressing.
"By one who acts with care" means by one who acts without fail in performing what is beneficial, teaching what is beneficial, and intending what is beneficial.

‘If he falters, he should be supported in accordance with the Dhamma’: when the pupil falters, whether from correct practice or from improper speech, he should be supported—by means of the appropriate reason—in accordance with the Dhamma, that is, by his own nature, in the virtues such as morality and so forth.
‘The Meṇḍaka questions, the profound, knotty, and secret questions’:
for the sake of the increase of the scriptures, practice, and the Dispensation, he exerts effort through means such as the giving of the four requisites.
"He is one who shares equally with the Saṅgha in both happiness and suffering, and who is governed by the Dhamma;
he is a sharer according to his ability, a promoter of the Victor’s Wheel,
one who prioritizes right view, and likewise one who has no other support."
"Guarded in bodily action and the rest, delighting in harmony, free from debt, not a slave,
possessing the wheel [of sovereignty], having gone for refuge to the Buddha and the others—
these ten qualities of a lay follower were spoken by Nāgasena."
These are the three verses:
“The fifth [syllable] is light in all cases; the seventh in both the second and fourth [feet];
but the sixth is considered a heavy syllable; the remaining [positions] are considered unrestricted.”
It is described by the characteristics stated herein.
"Common to the world" means similar to the world of sentient beings.
"Of those who have not attained the mind" refers to those who have not reached the fruit of Arhatship.
"By means of the object that is the jewel of knowledge": the Blessed One possesses the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutā-ñāṇa*) which has the path of arahantship as its proximate cause;

he is all-knowing, all-seeing, endowed with the ten powers (*dasabala*), possessed of the four kinds of intrepidity (*vesārajja*), one who has broken through the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), a possessor of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), one whose knowledge is uncommon, and one endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha. His is the knowledge of the path of arahantship.

"Bestowing all qualities such as the ten powers" refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*), which is the means for knowing all knowable phenomena. "By each respective arising of consciousness having the jewel of the Blessed One’s knowledge as its object" [is said].
"'Are being uprooted' means they are being overturned from their natural state or are perishing."

"Having encountered that most excellent leader of the assembly, the false-seeing heretics have become lusterless"—this is the construction: having encountered the Blessed One, that most excellent leader of the assembly, who is supreme among the leaders of assemblies, the heretics—who are holders of wrong views—become lusterless, devoid of light.
In the *Meṇḍakapañha*, the first question, concerning "the bound by honor and the bound by non-honor," together with its eight similes, concludes here.
"O Great King, a hundred cartloads of rice, and a half-cartload less a small measure, seven measures of rice, and two *tumba* measures [would be consumed] in a single moment."

Regarding the statement, "If one were to establish a limit for the amount of wealth currently circulating, saying 'it is this much,' it would reach exhaustion and depletion," it is stated in the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*:
"In this context, one hundred and fifty cartloads (*vāha*)—with a small portion added to the falling away of half a hundred cartloads—is called a 'tumbo'.
Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that an "aḍḍhacūḷa" is a cartload plus half a cartload.
One *kuḍuba* is one *pasata*; four of those would be an *āḷhaka*.
Four *āḷhakas* are a *doṇa*, and four *doṇas* are a *māṇikā*. Four *māṇikās* are a *khārī*.
"Twenty khāris make a vāha; ten ammaṇas make a tumba;
a tumba is always an āḷhaka; a patha is a nāḷi for women;
a vāha is a cart-load (ceka); ten doṇas make an ammaṇa."
In the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, it is stated that "a *vāha* is the measure of a cart-load";
however, in the *Vinaya-ṭīkā*, it is stated that "two cart-loads are one *vāha*. A hundred *vāhas* less a half-peak (*aḍḍhacūla*) means a hundred *vāhas* less by a half-peak;
that is, it is slightly less than a half-peak. It refers to seventy *vīhi*-grains more than the aforementioned *vāha*. As for the *vīhis*:
The construction is: "There were seven *ammaṇas* and two *tumbas*. The intended meaning is "more than one hundred and two-and-a-half cartloads of rice.

This [word] is connected with the word "of" (*imassa*) in the phrase "of the consciousness occurring in a single moment of a finger-snap" (*ekaccharakkhaṇe pavattacittassa*). The term *lakkhaṇa* has the sense of grasping or discerning;

here it is used in the accusative case in the sense of the dative. [In the phrase] "he entered for his midday rest" (*divāvihāraṃ pāvisī*), [it means] "for the purpose of a midday rest" (*divāvihārathāya*).
As in the case of *pāvisitī* and so forth. Furthermore, the word *lakkha* denotes a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). For this has been stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*:
“A spot, a mark, a sign, a brand, a token, a distinguishing mark, a characteristic, and also a symbol;
moreover, it is supreme beauty when perfectly well-proportioned.”

“Exhaustion” (*parikkhaya*) and “termination” (*pariyādāna*) mean that they would reach a state of being destroyed. By this, he shows that within a single moment of time (*ekaccharakkhaṇa*), there are more thoughts than one hundred and ten *vīhi*-grains.

Having thus shown the manifold nature of the thoughts occurring in a single moment of time by way of such a number of *vīhi*-grains, he now says, “In this regard, these... and so forth, in order to show the specific distinction of the thoughts occurring in a single moment of time according to the particularity of the individual (*puggala*).
Likewise...
Therein, "among beings" means among the seven kinds of beings.
"These seven kinds of consciousness proceed" means these seven types of consciousness function.
"Uncultivated in body" means they have not cultivated the body—namely, the five aggregates of clinging—with respect to impermanence and so forth.
“Of undeveloped virtue” means those whose supramundane virtue is undeveloped.

“In three places” refers to the three places by way of the eradication of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*). “In the higher planes” refers to the higher planes consisting of the five aggregates of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) and so forth.
“In five places” should be understood as the five places consisting of the three places mentioned below, with the addition of the two stages of the thinning of lust and hatred (*rāgadosatanuṭṭhāna*).

"In ten places" refers to the five lower stages already mentioned, by way of the eradication of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) known as personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, greed, and ill-will;
and by way of the eradication of the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana).
"Another five" should be understood as the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) themselves, which serve as the objects for insight (vipassanā). Thus, there are ten places.
‘A steel arrow’ means an iron shaft with a point inserted at its tip.
‘Fixed upon a strong bow’ means mounted upon a firm bow or crossbow.
‘Thus’ refers to the Blessed One’s swift maneuvering. ‘A further feat’ refers to what was spoken as being superior to the Twin Miracle.

That too, O Great King, is a miracle (*pāṭihīra*). That Twin Miracle of the Blessed One—consisting in the simultaneous issuing of flames and streams of water—is a miracle because it removes passion and other opposing defilements from oneself and others.
"By a mere act of adverting" refers to the second question on omniscience, which concerns the inferiority of mind-door adverting that has not been produced by the Blessed One.
"When six divisions are made in the aeon": when six divisions are made in the aeon of the period of expansion and stability, which measures sixty-four intermediate aeons (*antarakappa*).

When the first division has passed—meaning when more than ten intermediate aeons have elapsed, having passed the first division of the aeon of the period of expansion and stability—Devadatta split the Saṅgha. This concludes the third question regarding Devadatta’s going forth, within the section on Restraints.
"That which depends on the body as its means and is eternally composed of karma is *yama*;
that which comes from external means and is non-eternal would be *niyama*.
Non-violence, truthfulness, contentment, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—"
"Constant bodily purity is called 'Yama'; contentment, silence, recitation,
the practice of austerity, meditation, living in the forest of self-cooking,
and the observance of rules constitute constant discipline."

When this was said regarding the twin miracles (*yamakamma*) and the miracle of constraint (*niyamakamma*): "That which the Tathāgata... [as before] ...such is his intention" (*evamadhippāyo*). The construction is as follows: "There exists that marvelous quality of the Buddhas, by virtue of which quality acting as a cause... such is the intention.
"Exertion was demonstrated" means that the exertion (*parakkama*), the effort (*vāyāma*) in fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*), was demonstrated and made visible.
"Today they have been illuminated": the perfections (*pāramī*) and methods (*naya*) of the Victors have been illuminated even more, with exceeding excellence.

"The knot of the doctrines of the sectarians has been split": you have split that knot of false doctrine belonging to the sectarians. "The jars of the opponents' arguments have been shattered": the opponents' arguments have been shattered by you.
"Profound, yet made shallow": this question, which is exceedingly profound, has been made shallow by you.

"The means of removal rightly obtained by the sons of the Conqueror": the method of removal known as a skillful means for taking away the doctrine of supreme error has been well-obtained by the sons of the Conqueror among the sons of the Conqueror.
"It is so": all that has been stated below is exactly as it was spoken by you.
The phrase "all speech is thus by its very nature" is an ellipsis to be supplied;
"O best and most excellent of leaders" is an address to the leaders and their assemblies, meaning:
"O most supreme one, we accept exactly as you have spoken."
The Fourth Question on the Cause of the Earth’s Quaking.
“Nathaññaṃ ceta” means that among these truths, there is no other cause existing as a truth for the penetration [of those truths].
“By Sīharatha” means by the best chariot, the excellent chariot. For the word *sīha* (lion) or the word *usabha* (bull), when used in conjunction with another word, expresses the sense of "best."
The fifth question: The Supernormal Vision of King Sivi.

Regarding the statement "it descends into the *kalala*": this is said with reference to the blood, red as lac, that has accumulated in the place within the mother’s womb—situated between the backbone, the spinal cord, and the navel—which is fit for the implantation of the embryo and resembles a *kalala*. It does not refer to the material form (*rūpa*) of the *kalala* itself.

Regarding the statement "even by mouth-to-mouth contact there is a union of the two": even through mouth-to-mouth contact, there occurs a "union of the two" in the sense that "the mother is in her season and the womb is prepared."

"I shall likewise state the reason by means of the former" means that I shall explain the logical statement regarding the reason why those two or three conjunctions are included within the lineage of Sāma.
"All those" refers to whatever beings have entered a mother’s womb; the construction is: "all those beings [are like] the forest trees and so forth.
"Any creature whatsoever" refers to any being who, through his own karma, has come to be born in such and such a way.
The sixth question: On the Entrance into Non-existence.

"The True Dhamma" refers either to the True Dhamma of attainment belonging to those who have destroyed the taints and reached the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), or to the True Dhamma of penetration by way of the reversal of the pure method.
"Manifesting that destruction" means manifesting, by that statement, the destruction of the True Dhamma which was capable of lasting for five hundred years.

“He delimited the remainder” means he delimited the remainder as the period of five hundred years during which the true Dhamma remains. Showing both the manner of its illumination and the manner of its delimitation, he said: “A hundred years, a thousand,” and so forth.
“One whose wealth is lost” means one whose property has been destroyed.
This is the seventh question concerning the measure of five hundred years.
Regarding this, it is written in the manuscripts: "Those beings whom karma afflicts, those beings ward off the cause;

their statement is false. This is difficult to understand. Therefore, those beings whom karma afflicts are born from the ripening of karma and experience painful feelings; as for those beings who ward off the cause... [their statement is false].
The reading should be "that statement is false. For it is only thus that the preceding and following parts cohere.
In that context, regarding those ninefold [types], among the ten types of turbulent winds, those which are the ninefold turbulent winds do not arise in the past;
that is, those winds do not arise in a past existence through the power of karma. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well.
"By various kinds of cold, etc. means by those various modes of disturbance such as cold and so forth.
"Each its own feeling" means the feeling that has become the fruit for each individual.
"Born from uneven postures" means the feeling produced from the irregular shifting of the four postures.
"By means of an assault" (*opakkamika*) means by the assault of another, such as the striking of a blow.
"Born of the ripening of karma" (*kammavipākaja*) means born from the five aggregates that constitute the ripening of karma.
"The remainder is more abundant" means that the feeling remaining after the feeling born of the ripening of karma is more abundant.
"It does not come to pass" means it does not succeed.
"Defectiveness of the seed" refers to being defective due to the field or other causes.
"Or from the ripening of kamma"—in this context:
“In the past, for the sake of wealth, I killed my half-brother.
By the ripening of that kamma, Devadatta hurled a rock;
a stone fragment crushed my toe.”

This verse should be stated as "for the sake of wealth" (*tatha dhanahetu*), meaning for the sake of movable wealth consisting of male and female slaves. For wealth is fivefold, by way of: fixed wealth, movable wealth, portable wealth, wealth that is like a limb, and accompanying wealth.
Or, "due to action" (*kiriyato vā*) means due to Devadatta’s act of violence.
"Food transforms abnormally" (*bhojanaṃ visamaṃ pariṇamati*) means the food that has entered the stomach undergoes an abnormal state of digestion.
And regarding the phrase "by that feeling," this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the agent (*kattari karaṇavacana*).

Regarding the term "the excellent sect-mark" (*nikāyavara-lañchaka*): here, they mark or identify themselves by means of it; or alternatively, the wise mark their merits and demerits by it, thus it is a "marker. The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both an excellent sect and a marker.
This is the eighth question, on the burning away of all unwholesome states.
In this question, the Elder did not provide a categorical answer. Therefore, one should investigate and accept that which is more logical.

This is the manner of investigation: for those defilements subject to abandonment by the Path are non-clung-to (anupādinnaka), being neither past, nor future, nor present. And the discussion regarding the cessation of what is clung-to refers to future existence.
The pain experienced by the Blessed One was said to have arisen in this very present existence alone.
