Furthermore, even for Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, it is impossible to avert karma that is to be experienced in successive lives. Therefore, one should accept that the Elder’s statement, "This pain has arisen from the ripening of past karma," is more appropriate. If this is so, why did the Elder [experience] manifold...
"How did he speak? [The answer is: "King Milinda, seeking the penetration of knowledge and desiring to hear various inspired responses, spoke according to his own inclination;
thus, in such instances, one should state the explanation as follows:
'One must seek the underlying logic itself, rather than being a person of a single fixed thought.'"
"Accumulation of what has been done": there is no further increase or accumulation of the sixteen duties performed regarding the Four Truths.
"It must be extinguished" means it must be unraveled and explained. "Seclusion" refers to the act of physical and mental seclusion.
Furthermore, in the sense of the term, the wholesome states such as concentration, mindfulness, and clear comprehension that are to be attained in the state of seclusion are called "seclusion."
"He protects" means he protects from the suffering of future states, such as the woeful realms and so forth.
This is the ninth question on seclusion.
"That power of supernormal success" refers to the state of being protected for aeon after aeon by means of that power of supernormal success.
"Even for as long as a finger-snap"—the intention is this:

even for the shortest possible duration, such as the time of a finger-snap, I do not praise the occurrence of existence (bhava) consisting of the five aggregates; rather, I praise only the non-occurrence that is Nibbāna.
The tenth question, on the Praise of the Power of Psychic Potency (*iddhibala*).
The commentary on the eighth chapter, adorned with ten questions, is completed.
"Monks, it is through direct knowledge that I teach the Dhamma"—thus [are taught] the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen...

I teach the Dhamma that has been known by omniscient knowledge through its specific distinctions, such as: the elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine roots, the four nutriments,
the seven groups of persons, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, and the seven types of consciousness.
"Another higher [training]"... "as far as the Satas" means another higher than the minor and secondary rules, namely the one hundred and fifty training rules consisting of:
four Pārājikas, thirteen Saṅghādisesas, thirty Nissaggiyas, ninety-two Pācittiyas, four Pāṭidesanīyas, and seven Adhikaraṇasamathas.
"Nor has it been decided by them as one" means it was not settled by their own minds with absolute certainty.
"By way of the stability of the Dhamma" means by way of the stability of the Dhamma as stated in the passage: "Whatever offense he has committed, he should be dealt with according to the Dhamma.
This is the first question concerning the abolition of minor and lesser rules.
"‘Is form impermanent? is a question to be answered by way of analysis. When asked, “Is that which is impermanent name-and-form alone, or is it only form?

one must answer by analyzing it according to the method beginning with, “Name-and-form is impermanent, and feeling is also impermanent,” and so forth; thus it is called “to be answered by way of analysis.
Furthermore, regarding the question, “Does the person perceive everything with the eye?”—that is, “What does the person perceive with the eye?”—it is to be answered by way of analysis.

The construction of this passage is as follows: when asked by anyone regarding this question—“By which eye [do you see]? By the universal eye (samantacakkhu) or by the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu)?”—one should say, “Yes.
This is called a question to be answered by counter-questioning (*paṭipucchābyākaraṇīya*).
This is the second question of Māluṅkyaputta.
"The cause of fear has been eradicated by the Arahant": the cause of fear has been completely uprooted by the Arahant.
"Elevated and depressed": elevated by way of the state of elation in pleasure, and depressed by way of dejection in pain.
"In a person of crooked character": in a person who is manifestly wicked.
"Āhaccapada" refers to the words spoken by the Blessed One through the excellence of his omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
This concludes the third question regarding omniscience.
"By means of their occurrence" means by means of the occurrence of those powerful protective verses (*paritta*).
"Destroying the poison" means causing the poison to perish.
"Accumulating upwards and downwards" means increasing comfort throughout the upper and lower parts of the body.

Regarding the phrase "the club raised by enemies," it should be read as "the club raised by hostile thieves (*vericora*)," as it is written in the *Poṭhakas*; for it is not possible that a mallet (*muggara*) was raised by hostile thieves. Thus it is said.
‘Or he seeks for the purpose of food’ means he performs the function of eating.
‘By a needle’ means by the affliction of vomiting upwards.
‘By improper conduct’ means by a cause involving misconduct.

"O Great King, 'protection for beings' means, O Great King, that what is called a *paritta* (protective chant) is the further protection (*anurakkhana*) of those beings who are already being protected by [the power of] the *paritta*. The construction is:

'By what one has done oneself, one gains protection. This means that a person of evil character, through the fault committed by himself—such as through his own actions—loses and destroys the protective nature of the *paritta*.
This concludes the fourth inquiry: "The Inquiry into the Further Protection of Others’ *Paritta*."
The construction is: “And the power of Māra is not stronger than the power of the Buddha.
This is the fifth question, concerning the Five Sal trees.
In that regard, the phrase “there is a difference in meaning” means that there exists a distinction in meaning or a specific difference in meaning between those two statements.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*: “*Antara*, *majjha*, *vatha*, and *khaṇa*—these [terms] denote an interval; *okāsa* denotes a moment; and *hetu*, *vyavadhāna*, *vinā*, *bhedo*, and *chidda* denote absence.

“*Saññāvimokkho*” means liberation from the state of an offense by way of the presence of perception (*saññā*); that is to say, an offense involving consciousness (*sacittakāpatti*). “No saññāvimokkho” means there is no liberation from the state of an offense due to the absence of perception;
that is, non-liberation through perception (*nasaññāvimokkho*), meaning an offense without consciousness (*acittakāpatti*).
The sixth question: On Evil and Birth.
And regarding this question, O Great King—meaning this question asked by you—one part remains with a remainder;

that is, because of the statement beginning with “Ānanda, it occurs to the Tathāgata thus,” one part remains incomplete due to the remaining meaning consisting of the avoidance of the "flesh of men" (human flesh).
The seventh question: On Avoiding the Assembly.
"By what is taken up" means either by what is done or by hatred.
The eighth question: On the Indivisible Assembly.
The Second Chapter: Eight Questions.
Regarding "Yama is the best":
Yama is that which depends on the body as its instrument and consists of constant ritual action.
“Kamma is adventitious, impermanent, and subject to necessity in existence;
non-violence, truthfulness, self-restraint, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—
because they are to be accomplished constantly within the body, they are called ‘Yama.’”
Thus addressed, Yama said: "The best is self-restraint; the foremost is discipline.
Contentment, silence, recitation, and devotion to meditation are difficult to master.
“Dwelling in the forest of self-maturation and accomplishing the observances”—thus was the foremost observance spoken of.
Likewise, by the term “non-harming” (*ahiṃsā*), compassion (*karuṇā*) is expressed. “Truth” (*sacca*) refers to truthfulness of speech, truth of knowledge, and ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*).

"Ādheyya" refers to the state of being something to be placed; "brahmacārī" means abstention from sexual intercourse. "Apariggaho" expresses the state of being free from the craving for possession, thinking "this is mine.
"'Santosa-mona-sajjhāyā' refers to the twelve kinds of contentment that wash away evil, not merely the recitation of the Buddha’s words.
'Kicchāparo' refers to the observance of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga); thus, there are three types of development: preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā) and so forth."
"Residence in the Sayampāka forest": here, in this Sayampāka forest of the Buddha’s dispensation, the abstinence from Sayampāka must be undertaken. "In the manner of the beginning" means:
"Wandering" refers to wandering through village dwellings in accordance with the rules of the Sekhiya section.
"Dwelling" refers both to the dwelling in the postures of a true ascetic and to the threefold dwelling in the Dhamma by way of the divine, the brahma, and the noble [abidings].
“Self-restraint” means restraint of the sense faculties.
“Restraint” means restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
“Patience” means patience as endurance and patience as knowledge.
"The recitation of the training rules" refers to the canonical text (*pāḷi*) of the training rules.
"Learning and interrogation" refers to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the training rules.
By the phrase "the wearing of the saffron robe and the state of being a monk," he demonstrates the similarity between the two genders.
The intention is that he is either a brother with hair two finger-breadths long or one who is newly shaven.
“Restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), conduct (cāra) and likewise abiding (vihāra),
self-control (saṃyama) and restraint (saṃvara), as well as patience (khanti) and gentleness (soracca);”
Solitary wandering and delighting in solitude,
the practice of seclusion, moral shame and fear of blame;
heedfulness, energy, as well as recitation and interrogation.
Delight in virtue and so forth due to its nature of being without attachment,
and the fulfillment of the training rules—
these qualities that make one a recluse have been taught by Nāgasena in twenty divisions.
"Both the wearing of the saffron robe and likewise the state of being a mendicant—
these two characteristics of a recluse were taught by Nāgasena";
"one who has entered the state of a recluse" means one who has attained a state of similarity through these twenty qualities and two characteristics.
"Thus, 'recluseship' (sāmañña) means that state of being a recluse (samaṇabhāva). 'The foremost assembly' (aggaparisā) refers to the assembly known as the community of bhikkhus.
'That attainment has come to me'—among the twenty qualities and two characteristics, that attainment does not exist in me among beings.
This is the first question of the worldling (puthujjana).
"Those who are capable" means those beings who are fit and suitable.
This is the second question concerning the trickling of blood from the mouth.
"Resembling that" means similar to that which was previously hidden.
Regarding the statement "one administers an oil enema (anuvāsana)": the procedure for the rectum in the upper region is described in the *Āyurveda* as follows:
"Emesis, purgation, nasal medication, non-unctuous enema (nirūha), and oil enema (anuvāsana)—these five types of treatment are to be known; their specific application is now declared."
Enema treatment (*vasti-kamma*) is twofold, by way of *nirūha* (non-unctuous) and *anuvāsana* (unctuous).

Thus, the *nirūha* enema treatment should be administered in the lower part, via the path of excrement; the *anuvāsana* enema treatment should be administered in the upper part, via the path of urine.
Enema treatment and "super-enema" (*uttara-vasti-kamma*)—these two names refer to those very same things.
They say: "What is its commentary?

(Instruction on Discipline): Any instruction concerning the restraint of defilements, evil, or persons—beginning with the entire *Vinaya Piṭaka*—is called "instruction on discipline" (*niggahadesanā*).

(Encouragement) Teaching that provides consolation, generates support, and praises the benefits of the path and moral virtue for the sake of dispelling fear in persons who are fearful is called *sampahaṃsanā*.

(Displaying the Purity of Conduct) Teaching connected with the entire *Jātaka*, beginning with the *Acchisutta* and including such discourses as the *Dvedhāvitakka* and the *Bodhirājakumāra*, is called *cariyāvodānanidassanā*.

(Answering Questions): The teaching beginning with the entire Sagāthavagga—starting from the Kūṭavimānasutta, the Vammikasutta, the Parāyaṇasutta, and so forth—which consists of answers to questions asked by the eight assemblies, is called "Answering Questions.
(Instruction): The teaching consisting of instructions on the Noble Lineages, the Accumulation of Merit, the Ascetic Practices, the Rules of Conduct, and related matters, is called "Instruction."

(Purification of the Person): The "Purification of the Person" (*puggalavisodhanā*) refers to those discourses connected with the teaching on the perception of danger—such as the *Devadūta*, *Aggikkhandha*, and others—which are spoken for the purpose of purifying the virtue, conduct, and so forth of individuals.

(Fulfillment of Inclinations): The "Fulfillment of Inclinations" (*ajjhāsayaparipūraṇā*) refers to discourses such as the *Tavaṭaka*, *Nāḷaka*, *Paṭipadā*, and *Dhammadāyāda*, which are taught for the purpose of fulfilling the serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) of individuals.

(The Discourse Showing the Succession): This is the discourse titled "Showing the Succession," which begins with the *Buddhavamsa* and the *Mahāpadāna-sutta*, and extends from the initial aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) of oneself and others up to their final *parinibbāna*.

(The Crushing of the Doctrines of Others): Beginning with the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, the teaching connected with the commentaries on the *Mahāsīhanāda*, *Cūḷasīhanāda*, and *Dhāna-bhiññā* is called "The Crushing of the Doctrines of Others.

(The Demonstration of the Requisite Condition): The teaching beginning with the *Itivuttaka* consists of the visible requisites (*upanissaya*) as they appear, presented through the body of what is currently manifest.

The demonstration of conditions (*paccayanidassanā*) consists of various discourses such as the *Dhaniyasutta*, the *Aruṇavatīsutta*, and the *Nādanapariyāyasutta*. (The demonstration of the manner of satisfaction:

*tuṭṭhākārasadassanā*) Teachings such as the entire *Udāna*, the *Sampasādaniya*, and the *Saṅgītisutta* are called the demonstration of the manner of satisfaction. (The demonstration of the qualities of the nature of phenomena:

*dhammasabhāvaguṇanidassanā*) These include the aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), faculties (*indriya*), truths (*sacca*), dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), the path (*magga*), the fruits (*phala*), and so forth.
The analysis of phenomena (*dhammavibhatti*) is the teaching of the Abhidhamma which illuminates both the similar and the dissimilar;

the teaching of characteristics (*lakkhaṇaparidīpana*) is that which illuminates the specific characteristics of those other phenomena which possess their own characteristics and are described according to their intrinsic nature.
By these fourteen modes, the Leaders of the World and their disciples teach the Dhamma. This is called the "Demonstration of the Qualities of the Nature of Phenomena."
Among those, the teaching by way of subsequent questioning (*pacchāvisajjanā*) is what is manifest here. The remaining [teachings] should be understood here according to their respective suitability.

(The Discussion on Being Subject to Offenses). "Conventional truth and ultimate truth—no third is found.

The statement, “O Brahmin, you ask about that which is insentient and does not hear... for what reason do you ask? was spoken with reference to the Palāsa Jātaka found in the Catukka Nipāta. Which Jātaka is that?
"O Brahmin, it is insentient"—this was said by the Deity while lying on his deathbed, referring to the Elder Ānanda:
"That venerable one was indeed myself as the tree deity.

“Thus even the *phadana* trees [spoke], those deities... [and so on] ... ‘Bhāradvāja, listen to me,’ it is said that they came. And this was spoken with reference to the *Phadana-jātaka* in the Thirteen-Nipāta.

Was this spoken by one dwelling in the Bamboo Grove with reference to the Mahākapi Jātaka, which was told in the *Tiṃsanipāta* concerning Devadatta’s hurling of the rock, saying:

Those who are here free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, and without taints;

“Those forest-dwellers, bearers of the ascetic practices, steadfast, wearing coarse robes,

All wear robes made of discarded rags and dwell in the City of Dhamma;
all wear the three robes with a piece of leather as the fourth;

Those who have few desires, who are prudent, steadfast, moderate in food, and free from greed;

Just as, upon seeing a well-proportioned and delightful city,

Likewise, the Buddha— who dispels sorrow,

Just as they know by inference that he who possesses such a radiance of Dhamma will become the supreme Buddha—

gentleness, solitary wandering, delight in solitude, seclusion, moral shame, moral dread, energy, heedfulness, the recitation of the training rules,
inquiry, delight in virtue and so forth, lack of attachment, and the fulfillment of the training rules— these twenty-two qualities that make one a recluse, along with the wearing of the saffron robe.
Including the two characteristics of "being a brother-in-law" (*bhaṇḍubhāva*), there are twenty-two qualities for the purpose of speaking [the *pātimokkha*].
25. One should understand the distinction between guarding and indulgence, as well as the heedful and the heedless; likewise, the opportunity for rest, illness, food, and what is obtainable.
One should share out the alms-food received, as well as comfort, the attendant, and the village residence.
Furthermore, one should engage in discussion; seeing a flaw, one should forgive it. One who acts with care and without breaking [the precepts] is worthy of two things:

the state of having no remainder and the state of being a producer. One should produce a mind that generates [virtue], expand the mind of one who is already expanded, and establish it in the strength of the training. One should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.
One should not abandon those who have fallen away, nor should one neglect the zeal for what ought to be done, nor the support, nor the harshness regarding the Dhamma.
"Thus, it is proclaimed as being embraced by twenty-five qualities"— this refers to the *Guṇapañcavīsaka* (Twenty-five Qualities) composed by a teacher for his pupil.
Anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, stubbornness, harshness, pride, arrogance, intoxication,
negligence, sloth and torpor, restlessness, indolence, evil friendship, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
"Wisdom, thirstlessness, and non-discontent"—these are the twenty-five qualities that weaken the mind; thus two sets of twenty-five have been stated.

28. Seclusion protects the person who is secluded. It increases longevity, it increases strength, it conceals faults, it removes ill-repute, it brings about renown, it removes discontent, and it brings about delight.
It removes fear, produces self-confidence, removes indolence, generates energy,
removes lust, removes hatred, removes delusion, destroys conceit, breaks off discursive thought, makes the mind one-pointed,
moistens the heart, generates joy, inspires reverence, arouses pride [in the noble], and is worthy of homage.

It produces [serenity], brings about rapture, generates gladness, reveals the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena, uproots the reconnection to existence, and bestows the commonality of all [noble ones].
This is the twentyfold set of qualities regarding seclusion.
O Great King, Mahosadha was brave, modest, conscientious, possessed of allies, endowed with friends, patient, and virtuous.
‘He is a speaker of truth, endowed with purity, free from anger, free from arrogance, not envious, energetic,
industrious, inclusive, generous, gentle, humble in conduct, honest, free from guile, endowed with intelligence,
renowned, endowed with knowledge, seeking the welfare of those who depend on him, handsome, beautiful to behold, learned by all people, wealthy, and famous.’”
This concludes the twenty-eight qualities of the great medicinal herbs; thus two sets of twenty-eight have been stated.

30. By means of these thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa)—having practiced them in the past, cultivated them, observed them, thoroughly mastered them, lived according to them, fulfilled them, and taken them as signs—the noble disciple here in this world becomes endowed with thirty excellent qualities.
By which thirty excellent qualities? He possesses a mind that is affectionate, soft, gentle, and full of loving-kindness;

he has destroyed, struck down, and eliminated the defilements; he has slain and subdued pride and arrogance; he possesses unwavering, firm, well-established, and confident faith; he is perfected and satisfied.

He is a recipient of the attainment of peaceful happiness characterized by joyful greedlessness; he is thoroughly imbued with the excellence, preeminence, incomparability, purity, and fragrance of virtuous conduct (*sīla*).
He becomes dear and pleasing to gods and humans; he is established as a noble person whose taints are exhausted; he is praised, honored, extolled, lauded, and glorified by gods and humans;
he remains unsullied by the world, whether here or hereafter; he perceives danger even in the slightest fault;
he is the means for attaining the excellent goal of the paths and fruits for those desiring vast and supreme success; and he partakes of abundant and exquisite requisites offered without being asked.
One who dwells without a home, who abides in the supreme dwelling of meditative concentration, whose foundation of the net of defilements has been disentangled,

who has broken, shattered, crushed, and destroyed the obstacles to progress, whose nature is unshakable, whose dwelling is not led astray, who enjoys blameless wealth, who is liberated from rebirth, who has crossed over all doubt,

whose self is absorbed in liberation, who has seen the Truth, who has attained the firm refuge that is immovable, whose underlying tendencies are utterly severed, and who has reached the destruction of all taints.
Abounding in dwelling in the attainment of peaceful happiness, and endowed with all the qualities of a recluse—he is thus endowed with these thirty excellent qualities.
Thus ends the Thirtyfold Set of Excellent Qualities and Benefits of the Ascetic Practices (dhutaṅga).
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow is suffering, lamentation is suffering...
Suffering and despair, association with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant, the death of a mother, the death of a father,
the death of a brother, the death of a sister, the death of a kinsman, the loss of kinsmen, the loss of wealth, the loss of virtue,
the loss of right view, the calamity of kings, the calamity of thieves, the fear of enemies, the fear of famine, and the fear of fire.
Suffering; the fear of water, the fear of waves, the fear of whirlpools, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of sharks,
the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of ill repute, the fear of punishment,
the fear of an evil rebirth, the fear of timidity in assemblies, the fear for one’s livelihood, the fear of death, great terrors, and being flogged with canes.
They were beaten with whips, beaten with split-bamboo canes;
they had their hands cut off, their feet cut off, their noses cut off, their ears cut off, or both their ears and noses cut off;

they were subjected to the *biḷaṅgathālika* torture, the *saṅkhamuṇḍika*, the *rāhumukha*, the *jotimālika*, the *hatthapajjotika*, the *erakavattika*, the *cīrakavāsika*, the *eneyyaka*, and the *balisamaṃsika* tortures.
The "sixtyfold suffering" consists of: being punished with a kahāpaṇa coin, being flayed with salt and lime,
being rolled over a crossbar, being placed on a bed of straw, being doused with boiling oil, being devoured by dogs, being impaled alive on a stake,
and having one's head cut off with a sword.

"Conch-shell shaven" (*saṅkhamuṇḍaka*) refers to the practice of making one's head like a conch shell. Those performing it cut the skin on both sides of the upper lip, bounded by the earlobes and the nape of the neck;
they gather all the hair together into a single knot, bind it with a cord, and pull it out.
The skin comes away along with the hair. Then, rubbing the skull with coarse gravel and washing it, they make it the color of a conch shell.
"Likewise, the *biḷaṅgathālika* (the 'sour gruel' torture)" refers to the performance of the sour-gruel ordeal.
While performing it, they gouge out the skull, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and insert it there. By that, the brain matter is cooked and rises to the surface.

"The mouth of Rāhu" refers to the performance of the Rāhu-mouth ordeal. While performing it, they open the mouth with a hook and light a lamp inside; or, starting from the temples, they carve the mouth with a chisel until blood flows and fills the mouth.
*Jotimālika*: wrapping the entire body in an oil-soaked cloth and setting it on fire.
*Hathapajjotika*: wrapping the hands in an oil-soaked cloth and setting them on fire.
*Erakavattika*: performing the "eraka-creeper" torture. While performing this, starting from the lower part of the belly, they wrap [the victim] in a coil of skin...
They pull [the skin] down to the ankles; then, having bound it with straps, they drag it.

He steps upon his own skin-cord and falls, crying out, "I am a wearer of bark garments!"—this is the "work of the bark-garment-wearer. While performing that work, they likewise pull the skin-cord and place it at the waist.
Having pulled it from the waist, they place it at the ankles. From the upper [cord], they [pull] the lower part of the body.
It is like being clothed in a garment made of bark-fiber.
"The Eneyyaka" refers to the Eneyyaka torture. While performing that, they drive iron spikes through both elbows, both knees, and the ankles;
he stands upon the ground supported by four iron spikes. Then, having surrounded him...
They set fire to it. Having removed the spears from the joints, they leave it standing on its eight bone-ends alone.
Regarding the "fish-hook-and-meat" torture: having struck with fish-hooks at both ends, they tear away the skin, flesh, and sinews. Regarding the "kahāpaṇa coin" torture:
they chop the entire body with sharp axes, shaving it off piece by piece the size of a kahāpaṇa coin, starting from the extremities.

"Khārāpatacchika" means that having struck the body here and there with weapons, they rub it with caustic lye using brushes; as the skin, flesh, and sinews ooze away, it remains standing like a skeleton of bones.

"Paḷighaparivattaka" means having made [the victim] lie on one side, they drive an iron spike through the ear-cavity and fix it firmly into the earth; then, seizing him by the feet, they spin him around.
"Palālapīṭhika" means that a skilled executioner, having sliced off the outer skin, splits the bones with small hammers and plucks out the tufts of hair.

"They seize them and toss them up; it becomes a mere heap of flesh. Then, wrapping them entirely in hair, they take hold of them and coil them around like a bundle of straw"—this is the *Vinaya-ṭīkā*.

Having observed this sixty-fold suffering, having become disenchanted with and detached from states of existence (*bhava*), and having abandoned craving for existence, one should contemplate the characteristic of suffering through the knowledge of the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā-ñāṇa*).
"Diyaḍḍhasikkhāpadasataṃ" means that one hundred and fifty training rules (sikkhāpada) should be understood by excluding the seventy-five rules of training (sekhiya) and taking the remainder.
This concludes the enumeration of the specific categories of numbers.

Regarding the one hundred and four items to be grasped, however, there are thirty-four with one meaning, thirty-four with two meanings, sixteen with three meanings, five with four meanings, thirteen with five meanings, and two with seven meanings.
The Commentary on the Milindapañha is completed.
Established in the wholesome,
the wholesome person attains the state of peace.
It was spoken by the Sage, well-expounded,
reaching the ultimate nature of things as they truly are;
it proceeds according to various underlying intentions.
Skilled in the study of the texts and having understood them,
one who speaks clearly should grasp the excellent meaning,
just as a lion seizes the king of elephants.
Just as one desiring health would reject what is harmful though it be pleasant,
so should the wise man accept a meaningful purpose even if it is unpleasant.
"Like a king of swans [to the water], like milk [to the water]"—[this refers to one] adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy;

endowed with a collection of virtues such as virtue, conduct, speed, and gentleness; possessed of the analytical power of wisdom capable of grasping and plunging into both his own system and other systems;
and possessing the unimpeded radiance of knowledge regarding the Teacher’s Dispensation, which is distinguished by the three Pitakas and the commentaries (Sāṭṭhakathā).
The Milindaṭīkā-gāthā, composed by the Elder Mahā-Acariya Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya— whose name was thus assumed by his teachers,
who was a preeminent debater and great poet endowed with vast and stainless wisdom,
and who spoke with the sweetness of a honeyed melody emerging from the bliss born of the perfection of his eloquent instruments— is hereby completed.
May he remain in the world for as long as he desires to deliver the world,
demonstrating to sons of noble family the purity of method and wisdom—
until even the name "Buddha" belongs to that one of pure mind who is such-like.
In this world, for the Great Sage, the eldest in the world,
twelve ambrosias were consumed; they destroy evil,
hunger, thirst, and even this [worldly] distress.
Anger, enmity, strife, and backbiting, as well as coldness and the like, bring about the attainment of the highest flavor;
yet for one who gives, they bring about results such as ripening and so forth.
But the well-spoken Dhamma destroys all defilements and,
beyond that, every evil without exception;
it brings to the giver the fruits of the stream-entry and other stages.
Thus, five hundred and fifty [monks],
endowed with a single flavor of sweet delight,
were well-prepared, virtuous, and well-perfected by Miliṇda.
By Nibhaya and Dvīpasena, who were disciplined and equanimous,
it was well-composed on the excellent island called Laṅkā,
in the Mahāvihāra, the abode of the Conqueror’s sons.
The succession of well-established groups of elders who illuminate this excellent Sāsana—
by means of being an ornament for them within the Sāsana, [I compose this].
To the one whose intellect is pure and purified regarding the Tipiṭaka,
who causes laughter along with men and kings,
and who causes laughter among the assemblies and the most excellent of groups;
This commentary, named *Milindapañhādīpikā*,
has been produced by me, a sprout of the Victor,
through the composition of verses according to the method of the Well-Gone One.
And whatever excellence of noble merit there may be,
by that very skill one should indeed set out upon the path;
among the three kinds [of persons], those who possess the noble knowledge of enlightenment—
Through fearlessness, may I swiftly attain that [state] and reach supreme omniscience; having passed away from here,
may I do so by means of wholesome karma.
I shall dwell in the city called Tusita among the devas,
practicing wholesome deeds again and again for a long time,
and likewise continuously in the presence of the excellent Metteyya.
Then, like a hero crossing over, the excellent sprout of the Conqueror—
just as the Heroic Buddha was— the sole leader of the world,
crossed over, performing sublime merit.
I am always honored by men and non-humans;
I am the excellent father-in-law, the noble-minded one, the giver of boons,
who dwells according to the Piṭaka as it was spoken among the people.
May you, the possessor of excellent, illuminating knowledge,
who seeks the supreme Dhamma and happiness, and who is virtuous,
[dwell] in the delightful Tusita heaven of the thirty-three gods.
I am born as one whose every wish is fulfilled,
always in an excellent and worthy place;
for the wise, who perform great meritorious deeds, are born thus.
I too am likewise in that supreme place,
honored by women and men,
distinguished by wealth, wisdom, and fame.
Purifying once again the teaching of the Teacher,
may I, by this merit, at the end of existence, attain the state of omniscience.
May I, well-intentioned and perfected in the pāramīs, become a constant doer of what is beneficial for the world in birth after birth through this vast merit, throughout all my existences.
May I become a Buddha, the most excellent one, far superior to men,
an abode of perfectly pure qualities nurtured by merit—
the supreme protector of protectors.
Through the merit performed by me with affection,
may those beings be free from enmity and happy;
may the gods and lords of men [protect] this entire earth.
"May those who possess the Dhamma protect [us] by means of the Dhamma and with impartiality."
